pages.transcription:
New York, 18.4.41.

Dear Manna & Manfred,
Yesterday your letter of Apr. 4th. I hope you
extended your Easter holiday in Bath until the end of this
week, and I wish you would remain there permanently. We
fully realise what advantages the degree of an X-Ray specialist
would mean to you, but at the moment the risks of the brutal
and indiscriminate air-raids over London seem great and we feel
anxious. - Eva has gone back to Croton yesterday. She was
happy to be with us and enjoyed the week in Newyork, but
she was looking forward again to the children and auntie
Olga whom she likes very much and of whom she talked with
great genuine affection. I am very glad about that, for she
really feels at home at Amity Hall and from all she told us
and from what we hear she has just that kind of care
and education you would like her to have. Mrs. Schaefer
probably will continue to try to explain you Eva's development
by using big words, but this means nothing more than a well-
meant effort for psychological description and has no connection
with her actual relations to the children. On the whole I en-
vied Eva for going back to the countryside and she will
enjoy the garden. I shall go out there one of the next sun-
days and have a look on it in springtime. Sunday Eva and
I will meet in Yonkers which is just halfway to Croton and
visit Elizabeth and her 11 year old girl. - Yesterday I sent
you a number of photos by air-mail, registered, to Bath,
and I hope you get them very soon. We find them excellent
and I hope you will not mind too much that Eva's hair is
not perfectly groomed. She had slept on it the wrong night side
the night before and the hair dresses could not do anything
about it in a hurry. The photo in hat and coat was Stefan's
idea. Eva thoroughly dislikes the hat which was bought by
Mrs Salmon and which is perfect American fashion for a
child of that age, and she at first refused that you should
even see it. But she won't wear it any more and it just
gives you an idea what Eva looked like this winter.
I am impatient to hear what you think of the photos.
We have ordered more and she will send some postcards too.

X I am afraid you will weep when you look at them like a
"slosh-kind"
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief auf zwei Seiten (hier Seite 1). Violette Tinte.
Rückseite des ersten Blattes, durchscheinender Text der Vorderseite sichtbar. Leer.

pages.transcription:
2)
I am sorry, Manna, that the news of my various complaints
upset you. Stefan really looked after me very well while I
needed it, and the calcium injections brought me back to
normal very quickly, and there are even nights again where I
don't wake up at all. As I wrote before, I am now being tested
thoroughly about my allergies by a specialist for allergics. The
tests will be finished soon, and the doctor promised to send
Manfred a report. I asked him to do so as I suppose you
would like a medical report. It seems that the Americans are
ahead in all those tests and the treatments, and they have
reason to do so as asthma is a wide-spread disease in both
North and South America. The chances of immunizing through
a kind of serum injections seem fairly good and you will
hear in due time. In any case I am quite well again and
there is no reason to worry. - But how is the health of you
both in those times? I believe I enquired several times
but you never even mention it. That is far more important
because of the heavy strain of the war.
We are very glad to be back in Newyork and
Newhaven had at least this good effect that I like New-
york again. We live very quietly and hardly see anybody.
It is a little enervating not to know where we will
be in two months time, but although some reasons speak
for returning to Brazil I am against deciding for such
a journey just now. Kindest regards to all, best love to you,
Lotte

Dear Hannah and Manfred, only good greetings
for today. My publisher Cassel wrote me that my account
for this taxation year shows £ 382/7/10, so you can
inform my accountant Binder & Hamlyn and must not go
to Cassels yourself. The idea of your going-around in
London is oppressive for us - you cannot imagine our rage
about this indiscriminate slaughtering of peaceful people. In
what ages are we living? Please tell to the widow of Max
Hermann-Neisse that I have written a obituary for him here
which has been published today, I hope I can send her a copy

{Randnotiz links:} of it. Lotte is not yet quite allright but we hope the treatment will bring
her not only momentary but durry relief from her
asthma - afars. Love all Stefan
